name: Small numbers
expr: [k for k in range(60) if is_prime(k)]
why: The primes below 60. 0 and 1 are not prime; 2 is.

name: A Carmichael number
why: False: 561 = 3 · 11 · 17. Fermat's test with any base that shares no factor with 561 says 'maybe prime' (MATH-5). Miller–Rabin with base 2 finds a square root of 1 that is not ±1.

name: More Carmichael numbers
why: All False. Each is a Carmichael number: it passes Fermat's test for every base with no common factor, but the strong test finds a witness.

name: Fools base 2
why: False: 2047 = 23 · 89 passes the strong test with base 2. A second base catches it.

name: Fools bases 2, 3, 5 and 7
why: False: 3,215,031,751 = 151 · 751 · 28351 passes the strong test for the four smallest prime bases.

name: Fools the first nine primes
why: False: it passes the strong test for every base from 2 to 23.

name: Fools the first twelve primes
why: False: the smallest number that passes the strong test for all twelve bases 2 to 37. Base 41 catches it, which is why the lesson uses 13 bases.

name: A big prime
why: True: 2⁶¹ − 1. Trial division would need about 1.5 × 10⁹ steps.

name: A square of a big prime
why: False: (10⁹ + 7)². No small factor, and trial division would need 10⁹ steps.

name: Two prime factors near 10¹²
why: False: the product of two primes just above 10¹².

name: Near 10²⁴
why: True: 10²⁴ + 7 is prime. pow(a, d, n) works with numbers this size directly.

name: Primes near 10¹⁸
expr: sum(1 for k in range(10 ** 18, 10 ** 18 + 20_000) if is_prime(k))
show: how many k from 10¹⁸ to 10¹⁸ + 19,999 have is_prime(k)
why: About 1 in 41 numbers near 10¹⁸ is prime (1 / ln 10¹⁸). Each test is a few modular powers.

name: Primes below 200,000
expr: sum(1 for k in range(200_000) if is_prime(k))
show: how many k below 200,000 have is_prime(k)
why: 17,984. Most numbers are thrown out by the small prime factors; each of the rest needs a few powers.
